units.title: Unit 13 — Thoughts and ideas
learningObjectives: Express confidence, uncertainty and differing opinions using advanced and register-appropriate lexical partnerships.
Distinguish sound judgement from poor decisions and avoid common errors with judgement collocations.
Interpret figurative collocations used for creative thought, persistent doubts and premature conclusions.
Select accurate prepositions and idiomatic verb partners when discussing beliefs and ideas.

items.example: I honestly think our proposal needs another round of testing.
items.note: Honestly or really can intensify think naturally; strongly think is not the usual pairing.

items.pt: pensar um pouco sobre alguma coisa
items.example: I will give your suggestion some thought before replying.
items.note: Give something some thought means consider it carefully rather than decide immediately.

items.pt: ter em mente; levar em consideração
items.example: Bear in mind that the results may change after calibration.
items.note: Use bear in mind to introduce a factor the listener should remember.

items.example: It is common knowledge that the road floods after heavy rain.
items.note: Common knowledge refers to information widely known within a group.

items.example: The trainees quickly grasped the importance of recording each measurement.
items.note: Grasp the importance means understand why something matters, not physically hold it.

items.pt: ser da opinião; adotar o entendimento
items.example: The committee takes the view that additional checks are necessary.
items.note: A rather formal alternative to believe, often followed by a that-clause.

items.example: The final vote was not a foregone conclusion despite the early predictions.
items.note: A foregone conclusion is an outcome regarded as inevitable beforehand.

items.pt: uma ideia aproximada; uma noção geral
items.example: We have a rough idea of the cost but still need quotations.
items.note: Rough means approximate or not fully developed; raw idea is not standard here.

items.pt: concordar com uma teoria; aderir a uma teoria
items.example: Some researchers subscribe to the theory that sleep improves learning.
items.note: Subscribe to a theory means accept or support it; the preposition is to.

items.example: There is a widespread belief that the old station is unsafe.
items.note: Widespread signals that a belief is held by many people, not that it is necessarily true.

items.example: Opinions are divided on whether the new timetable will help.
items.note: This impersonal phrase signals disagreement across people or groups.

items.example: She has a firm conviction that every student can improve.
items.note: Firm conviction denotes strongly held belief rather than evidence or certainty of outcome.

items.example: There are sound arguments for both proposed designs.
items.note: Sound modifies arguments to mean reasonable and well-founded, not loud.

items.example: My colleague takes a different view of the proposed solution.
items.note: Take a view is idiomatic; take an opinion is not the normal combination.

items.example: We could make a serious mistake if we ignore the warning.
items.note: Make a mistake is idiomatic; serious conveys the importance of its consequences.

items.pt: passar a perceber; tomar consciência de
items.example: Residents are becoming aware of the risks posed by the heat.
items.note: Become aware of is the natural change-of-state pattern; getting aware is atypical.

items.example: Please do not judge the new employee harshly after one mistake.
items.note: Harshly describes very severe or unforgiving judgement.

items.pt: falta de bom senso; julgamento ruim
items.example: Sending confidential information openly showed poor judgement.
items.note: Poor judgement describes an unsound evaluation or decision, not low-quality eyesight.

items.example: It would be unfair to pass judgement on her without the full report.
items.note: Pass judgement on somebody or something means evaluate or criticise, often prematurely.

items.example: He invested the money against his better judgement.
items.note: This expression means doing something despite believing it may be unwise.

items.example: The reckless decision revealed a lack of judgement.
items.note: Lack of judgement names an inability to make sound choices.

items.example: Approving the schedule without review was an error of judgement.
items.note: A more formal way to describe a decision based on a mistaken assessment.

items.pt: pensar de maneira criativa e não convencional
items.example: To solve the unusual problem, the team had to think laterally.
items.note: Thinking laterally means exploring unconventional approaches rather than linear ones.

items.example: Her fertile imagination made the workshop unexpectedly productive.
items.note: Fertile is metaphorical here, suggesting an abundant supply of original ideas.

items.pt: quebrar a cabeça com um problema
items.example: The engineers wrestled with a problem in the timing circuit.
items.note: Wrestle with means struggle mentally to reach an answer.

items.example: He had a nagging doubt about the accuracy of the estimate.
items.note: Nagging describes an unwelcome feeling that repeatedly returns.

items.example: The unexpected resignation fuelled speculation about a merger.
items.note: Fuel is a metaphor for causing rumours or conjectures to grow.

items.example: Do not jump to conclusions until we have checked the data.
items.note: Means form a judgement without enough facts; usually disapproving.

items.example: A fertile mind can find new uses for familiar tools.
items.note: Like fertile imagination, this is a metaphor for original ideas and creativity.

items.example: The preliminary findings fuelled a debate about public spending.
items.note: The figurative verb fuel can combine with debate and speculation.

items.pt: hesitar e refletir muito antes de decidir
items.example: She wrestled with a decision about moving overseas.
items.note: Wrestle with a decision is an extended metaphor for difficult consideration.

items.example: A nagging fear of failure kept him awake before the exam.
items.note: The adjective nagging combines naturally with fear, doubt and concern.

items.example: Unequal treatment can fuel resentment between colleagues.
items.note: Fuel resentment uses the same figurative pattern as fuel speculation, expressing growth in a negative emotion.

items.example: Ignoring the maintenance warning was a serious error of judgement.
items.note: Serious strengthens the consequences of the conventional error of judgement phrase.

items.example: The designers had to think outside the box to meet the budget.
items.note: Informal metaphor similar to think laterally; avoid overusing it in formal reports.

units.title: Unit 14 — Business reports
learningObjectives: Describe sales performance, competitive conditions and commercial strategy using idiomatic business collocations.
Explain financial pressure, production, stakeholders and company objectives with precise business register.
Report increases, decreases and trends using natural combinations of adjectives, verbs and nouns.
Identify misleading combinations such as high competition and strong increase and replace them with established terms.

items.example: The manufacturer announced record profits after a strong final quarter.
items.note: Record profits means the highest profit level reached so far, not merely strong sales.

items.example: A slight decline in demand led the shop to reduce its orders.
items.note: Slight decline describes a modest reduction; decline in demand takes in.

items.example: Small retailers face fierce competition from larger online businesses.
items.note: Fierce is idiomatic with competition; high competition is a poor direct substitute.

items.example: The sales team met its targets for the third quarter.
items.note: Meet targets means achieve planned goals; miss targets means fail to reach them.

items.pt: bem encaminhado para; perto de atingir
items.example: The charity is well on the way to reaching its funding goal.
items.note: Well on the way to expresses substantial progress towards a result.

items.example: The redesigned device is expected to go into production next spring.
items.note: Go into production means begin the manufacturing stage.

items.example: Better distribution could boost sales in smaller towns.
items.note: Boost commonly combines with sales, growth, confidence and profits.

items.example: The new investment aims to stimulate growth in the local economy.
items.note: Stimulate is a transitive verb here; stimulus is its noun form.

items.example: The council agreed to allocate a budget for building repairs.
items.note: Allocate means formally assign money or resources to a purpose.

items.pt: gerar mais negócios; atrair mais clientes
items.example: The expanded rail link may generate more business for local shops.
items.note: Generate business means produce commercial activity or new opportunities.

items.example: The product has several unique selling points, including lower energy use.
items.note: A unique selling point is a feature presented as distinguishing an offer from rivals.

items.pt: trazer benefícios no futuro; render bons frutos
items.example: Careful staff training will pay dividends over the coming years.
items.note: Figurative pay dividends means produce benefits later, not necessarily monetary payouts.

items.pt: fazer muito sentido do ponto de vista comercial
items.example: Replacing the old software would make sound business sense.
items.note: The fixed construction uses make, not do, business sense.

items.example: An independent researcher will chair the committee next year.
items.note: Chair functions as a verb meaning lead a formal group or meeting.

items.example: The factory needs to maintain quality while reducing waste.
items.note: Maintain quality is the natural phrase for preserving established standards.

items.pt: defender os interesses; promover os interesses
items.example: The association exists to promote the interests of small firms.
items.note: Promote the interests of a group means act in ways that support its concerns.

items.example: The new service was designed to satisfy the demands of commuters.
items.note: Satisfy the demands of is a formal way to describe meeting expectations.

items.example: The company identified young professionals as its target market.
items.note: Target market means the intended group of purchasers, not a geographic target alone.

items.example: The board must consider shareholder interests before approving the deal.
items.note: Shareholder interests are commercial or financial concerns of company owners.

items.example: The directors held an emergency meeting after the data breach.
items.note: Emergency meeting refers to a meeting called urgently because of a crisis.

items.example: A sudden hike in prices affected independent restaurants.
items.note: Journalistic and somewhat informal: hike implies a noticeable increase.

items.example: Rising energy bills could affect the bottom line this year.
items.note: The bottom line refers to a business’s net profit or final financial result.

items.example: The retailer operates on narrow profit margins during the winter.
items.note: Narrow profit margins mean limited profit compared with costs or revenue.

items.example: The management team set clear objectives for the next review.
items.note: Set objectives means establish intended outcomes; clear implies specific and understandable.

items.example: The theatre cut nonessential expenses to balance the books.
items.note: Means ensure income and expenditure can be brought into balance.

items.pt: solicitar a intervenção de administradores de insolvência
items.example: The struggling business had to call in the receivers after its debts mounted.
items.note: British insolvency expression for bringing in receivers to take control of assets.

items.example: Keeping prices stable will be a considerable challenge for suppliers.
items.note: Considerable modifies challenge to stress its substantial difficulty.

items.example: Part of the development budget was reserved for transport links.
items.note: A development budget funds planned improvements or projects.

items.example: The latest figures show a slight increase in online orders.
items.note: Use slight increase for a small change, not little increase.

items.example: The report recorded a slight decrease in maintenance costs.
items.note: Slight decrease is standard report style for a modest fall.

items.example: The service experienced a substantial increase in demand.
items.note: Substantial increase indicates a large measurable change; strong increase is less idiomatic.

items.example: The latest audit showed a substantial decrease in defects.
items.note: Substantial naturally modifies the size of a decrease.

items.example: Exports experienced growth following the trade agreement.
items.note: Markets and figures can show, see or experience growth; had growth is not standard report wording.

items.example: Monthly revenue figures show a rise compared with last year.
items.note: Show a rise is a normal reporting collocation for numerical changes.

items.example: The domestic market saw a decline in orders last autumn.
items.note: See a decline is metaphorical and typical of analytical business writing.

items.example: The larger plant’s output was five times greater than the smaller plant’s.
items.note: Use times greater than for quantitative comparisons in this source’s usage guidance.

items.example: Local providers now face intense competition in the digital market.
items.note: Intense is an accepted alternative to fierce or stiff when describing competition.

items.example: The applicant faced stiff competition for the research post.
items.note: Stiff competition is an idiomatic alternative to fierce competition.

items.example: The latest results confirm a rise in profits after restructuring.
items.note: Rise in is used before the quantity that grows, including profits or prices.

items.example: The new sales director expects to meet quarterly targets.
items.note: Quarterly specifies the time period over which targets are assessed.

items.example: Improved transport may act as a stimulus to growth.
items.note: Stimulus is a noun followed by to; stimulate growth is the corresponding verb pattern.
